<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: H.R. 4986, introduced by Rep. Mary Miller (R-IL), would amend PPRA to purportedly ``stand up for parental rights and create a barrier between our nation's schoolchildren and inappropriate influences from radical transgender ideology and Big Tech.''\25\ H.R. 4986 would require written consent before participation in each survey that touches on what Rep. Miller refers to as ``sexual orientation, gender identity, and woke politics,''\26\ and in so doing it changes participation in these surveys. For surveys given as part of a program administered by ED, it would eliminate the annual written consent and require repeated consent for each survey; for surveys not part of such a program but in an LEA that receives federal funds, it would change the survey from opt-out to opt-in.\27\ While the Majority claims this is to protect parents' rights because schools ``force sexual materials or political ideology upon children while keeping parents in the dark,''\28\ it is clear that is not how school surveys are conducted. Instead, H.R. 4986 is yet another attempt to scapegoat transgender students as an excuse to undermine public education. H.R. 4986 would harm all students by reducing school, district, and state awareness of school climate, mental health, and other issues and limit the ability of schools, districts, and states to support students in addressing their needs.
\25\Press Release, Rep. Miller Sponsors Legislation to Protect our Schoolchildren from Dangerous Influences from Radical Transgender Ideology and Big Tech, Office of Congresswoman Mary Miller (Feb. 15, 2023), https://marymiller.house.gov/media/press-releases/rep-miller-sponsors-legislation-protect-our-schoolchildren-dangerous.
\26\Id.
\27\See infra text accompanying notes 37 & 38.
\28\Press Release, supra note 25.
H.R. 4986 WILL HINDER STATES', DISTRICTS', AND SCHOOLS' ABILITIES TO
ASSESS AND ADDRESS SCHOOL CLIMATE AND YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH
Research shows that students who feel safe and supported at school have better educational outcomes. As the Learning Policy Institute highlighted, ``[p]ositive school climates are associated with increased academic achievement and attendance, higher graduation rates, improved behavior, and lower teacher attrition rates.''\29\ Over the years, the U.S. Department of Education has supported improving school climate.\30\ The National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) at the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) ``prioritized research about school climate and the use of such research to develop more effective policy and school practices,'' including publishing a series of school climate surveys for use by states, districts, and schools.\31\
\29\Learning Pol'y Inst., Using Data to Improve School Climate: Fact Sheet (Nov. 2024), https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4488/ download?inline&file=Data_School_Climate_FACTSHEET.pdf.
\30\See, e.g., the School Climate Transformation Grant program, which provided grants to LEAs (https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/ grants-birth-grade-12/safe-and-supportive-schools/school-climate-transformation-grant-local-educational-agency-lea-grants-program) and State Educational Agencies (SEAs) (https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/grants-birth-grade-12/safe-and-supportive-schools/school-climate-transformation-grant-state-educational-agency-grants-program), the Safe and Supportive Schools (S3) grant program (https:// www.cde.ca.gov/ls/ss/se/safesupportive.asp), and the former National Center on Safe and Supportive Learning Environments (https:// www.air.org/project/school-climate-survey-compendium and https:// www.schoolsafety.gov/resource/national-center-safe-and-supportive-learning-environments), as well as other efforts of the Office of Safe and Supportive Schools (OSSS)_and its predecessor, the Office of Safe and Healthy Students (OSHS)_within the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education (OESE) (https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-offices/oese/ safe-and-supportive-schools).
\31\Nat'l Ctr. for Educ. Statistics, Inst. of Educ. Sciences, ED School Climate Surveys (EDSCLS), https://nces.ed.gov/use-work/ elementarysecondary/ed-school-climate-surveys-edscls (last visited July 22, 2026).
For surveys conducted as part of a program administered by ED, PPRA already requires that the annual parental notice and consent for surveys discussed above (that touch on one of the eight enumerated topics) be in writing, but it does not require the annual notice and consent by emancipated or adult students be in writing.\32\ H.R. 4986 would amend PPRA to require that both be in writing. In and of itself, this is not an objectionable amendment to the law. However, H.R. 4986 goes further by requiring that written consent be given for each survey rather than a general annual consent currently permitted under the law. H.R. 4986 would also require written consent for each such survey given by an LEA that receives federal funding (even if the survey is not given under a program administered by ED), changing the law from a parental opt-out provision to a parental opt-in provision.
In her own words, Rep. Miller stated that the bill was introduced to specifically target surveys related to sexual orientation and gender ideology.\33\ However, it is worth noting that nothing in H.R. 4986 limits its scope to surveys involving sexual orientation or gender identity. The effect of the bill would be much broader and could significantly reduce survey responses on state/district/school climate surveys and other surveys, including the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) voluntary, biennial Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS). The YRBS is part of the CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS) and has been conducted since 1991 using a sampling of 9th through 12th graders.\34\ It ``measures health-related behaviors and experiences that can lead to death and disability among youth and adults,'' the results of which can be used to ``help monitor health trends, identify emerging issues, and plan and evaluate programs that can help improve adolescent health.''\35\ The CDC uses the YRBS to understand health-related behaviors and also issues such as weight, obesity, and asthma.\36\ According to the CDC, requiring opting-in for the YRBS could have significant detrimental consequences:
\32\20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232h(b).
\33\Supra note 25.
\34\Nancy D. Brener et al., Overview and Methods for the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System--United States, 2023 3, U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) (Oct. 10, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/ volumes/73/su/pdfs/ su7304-H.pdf.
\35\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS): About YRBSS (June 14, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/about/index.html.
\36\Laura Kann, et al., Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance--United States, 2017 3, U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) (June 15, 2018), https:// www.cdc.gov/mmwr/ volumes/67/ss/pdfs/ss6708a1-H.pdf.
Active parental permission typically requires more
time and resources and may reduce the number of
students who participate in the survey because of the
difficulty of both getting permission forms home to
parents and having forms returned to school. As a rule,
expect the use of active parental permission to reduce
student response rates by about 50 percent unless you
implement the following steps to help maximize student
participation:
• Mail or email permission forms and
information about the survey directly to parents.
• Emphasize the importance of the survey to
teachers and ask them to remind students to return the
permission forms to school.
• Telephone or email parents to follow up on
missing permission forms.\37\
\37\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS): A Guide to Conducting Your Own Youth Risk Behavior Survey 3 (Sept. 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/ media/pdf/ 2023/2023_yrbs_conducting_your_own.pdf.
In fact, opt-in requirements generally hinder participation in surveys in general, and they also affect who participates in the survey.\38\ For example, in a school setting, an opt-in requirement for each survey may make it less likely that working parents or parents who speak a different language submit the written consent.
\38\Yvonne de Man et al., Opt-In and Opt-Out Consent Procedures for the Reuse of Routinely Recorded Health Data in Scientific Research and Their Consequences for Consent Rate and Consent Bias: Systematic Review, 25 J. Med. Internet Res. 1, 18 (2023), https:// pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ articles/PMC10015347/pdf/ jmir_v25i1e42131.pdf (``[C]onsent rates are lower in studies using opt-in procedures. . . In addition, in studies using an opt-in procedure, consenters are more likely not to be representative of the study population compared with studies using an opt-out procedure.'').
Committee Democrats agree it is imperative that parents be aware of what is happening in their child's school. Current law strikes a reasonable balance between requiring both parental notification and annual written consent while permitting parents to opt their child out of these surveys on the one hand and the importance of conducting such surveys for the success of students on the other. Upsetting this balance and requiring parents to opt-in for each survey likely means that far fewer students may be participating in surveys for reasons other than the survey subject matter. This will hinder the collection of research used to understand the health, mental health, and safety of students and the development of programs and supports to benefit our nation's youth, with no material increase in parents' rights.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 4986
Committee Democrats did not offer any amendments to H.R. 4986.
CONCLUSION
As described above, H.R. 4986 would make it more difficult for schools and districts to conduct surveys, including mental health surveys, under the guise of parents' rights and would replace the balanced approach to parents rights and gathering data using surveys under current law, making it harder for schools to collect critical information on student mental health, school climate, and safety while offering no new rights for parents. All Committee Democrats present at the markup opposed H.R. 4986 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on July 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
John Mannion,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.
